description_intro: The South Sea Bubble of 1720 fooled even Isaac Newton. He sold his shares early at a profit, then bought back near the top and lost around a third of his fortune. This is the true story of how a company built on government debt became a mania, how it crashed, and the money lesson it still teaches.

scenes.say: London, the summer of seventeen twenty. The greatest scientist alive, Sir Isaac Newton, is about to make a terrible decision. Months earlier, he sold his shares and walked away with a large profit. Now he is buying them back, at prices close to the highest they will ever reach.
By the end of the year, the bubble had burst, and almost his entire fortune was tied up in that one company.
So why did the man who explained gravity go back in? How much did he really lose? And did he ever say the famous line people still quote about it? Let's go back to the South Sea Bubble.

The story begins with a problem every government knows: debt. In the early seventeen hundreds, Britain had borrowed heavily to pay for its wars. In seventeen eleven, a new company was founded to take over part of that debt. Its main founder was Robert Harley, the Lord Treasurer, the head of the government's money.

The idea sounded clever. People who were owed money by the government could swap what they held for shares in the new company. The government paid the company interest. And in return, the company got a promise of riches: the right to trade with Spain's colonies in South America. That is why it was called the South Sea Company.

But there was a dark side, and a weak one. Much of that trade was the trade in enslaved African people, and even that was limited by Spain. The great South American riches never really came. On paper, it was a trading company. In practice, it was a company that held government debt.
That should have been the end of the excitement. Instead, in seventeen twenty, it became the beginning.

In the spring of seventeen twenty, Parliament accepted a much bigger plan. The South Sea Company would take on a huge part of the national debt, in exchange for new shares. The more the share price rose, the better the deal looked for the company. So the company did everything it could to make the price rise.

It sold new shares in instalments, so you only paid part of the price at first. And it lent people money to buy its own shares. Think about that. The company was lending you the money to push up its own price.
At the start of seventeen twenty, one share cost about one hundred and twenty-eight pounds.
By the summer, it had passed one thousand pounds. Lords, merchants, shopkeepers and servants crowded into Exchange Alley in the City of London to buy. Even King George the First owned stock.

Imagine being there. Your neighbour bought in spring and has already doubled his money. Your cousin borrowed to buy, and now he is talking about a new carriage. Every coffee house is full of the same question: how high can it go? Nobody wants to be the only fool who stayed out.

And it was not only the South Sea Company. Dozens of new companies appeared, promising almost anything: trading in hair, getting silver out of lead, even a wheel that would turn forever. Most of them had no real business at all.
Isaac Newton watched all of this from a very special position.

Newton was not just a scientist. Since sixteen ninety-nine, he had been Master of the Royal Mint, in charge of Britain's coins. He earned well, he invested carefully, and before the bubble he was worth a little over thirty thousand pounds. In today's money, that is a rich man.

Early in the mania, he seems to have decided it would end badly. In April seventeen twenty, within about a week, he sold almost all of his South Sea shares, at a large profit. A careful, rational decision. If the story ended there, we would call him a genius of money too.
But it did not end there. The price kept climbing. Through May. Through June. People he knew were getting richer every week. Staying out began to feel like losing.

In the middle of June, Newton went back in. He bought again, now at prices close to the peak. And he kept buying through the summer, even when the price was starting to slip. By the time the crash came, almost all of his wealth was in South Sea stock.

Think about how that feels. When you sell and the price keeps rising, you do not feel careful. You feel foolish. Every new high is a small punishment for being right too early. Newton felt that punishment for two months. Then he gave in.

Not everyone made his mistake. A London bookseller named Thomas Guy had also bought South Sea shares. In seventeen twenty, while prices were still high, he sold, and kept his profit. He used much of that fortune to found a hospital in London. Guy's Hospital still carries his name today.
Two men, one stock. One sold and stayed out. The other sold, then could not stand to watch from the side. So what happened when the music stopped?

In September seventeen twenty, the price collapsed. There was no real business underneath to hold it up, and once enough people wanted to sell, nobody wanted to buy. By the end of September, the share that had passed one thousand pounds was worth less than two hundred.
By December, it was down to about one hundred and twenty-four pounds. Lower than where the year began.

A young engraver named William Hogarth turned the madness into a picture. In his print, investors ride a merry-go-round under a sign that asks: who'll ride? Around them, the city has lost its mind. It was one of the first great satires of a stock market crash.

Many people who had bought late, often with borrowed money, were ruined. The public was furious. An inquiry found that government ministers had taken bribes in the form of shares. The company's cashier, Robert Knight, fled abroad. And the Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Aislabie, was sent to the Tower of London.
The man who calmed the storm was Robert Walpole, who had opposed the scheme. The crisis carried him to power, and he is usually called Britain's first prime minister.

But here is something the popular story leaves out. Historians like Helen Paul point out that the damage to Britain's wider economy was much smaller than legend says. The company itself carried on for many years afterwards. The pain fell hardest on the people who bought late, near the top. People exactly like Isaac Newton.

And Newton? A famous story says he lost twenty thousand pounds. But the economist Andrew Odlyzko studied Newton's accounts, and he estimates the real loss at about ten thousand pounds. That is still around a third of his fortune, and all of his early profit, gone.

Newton himself wrote, in a letter in seventeen twenty-four, that he had lost very much by the South Sea company. And the famous line? That he could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people? It is quoted everywhere, but there is no solid proof he ever said it. Treat it as a legend.
So what can a crash from three hundred years ago teach us today? This is not financial advice. It is a lesson from history.

First: being smart does not protect you from a crowd. Newton understood the universe. He even saw the danger early. What beat him was not a lack of brains. It was the feeling of watching other people get rich without him.

Second: decide your exit before you buy, and then keep your word to yourself. Newton's first decision was good. His second one, made in the heat of the summer, undid it. Thomas Guy's plan was boring, and it built a hospital.

Third: when a price rises only because people expect it to keep rising, and buyers are borrowing to join in, be careful. Ask what is really underneath. In seventeen twenty, the honest answer was: not much.

Fourth: do not keep everything in one basket. By the end of seventeen twenty, almost all of Newton's wealth sat in one company. Afterwards, he slowly moved about half of it into Bank of England stock. He learned to spread his risk, but only after paying for the lesson.

Bubbles still happen. The names change, the story stays the same: a new kind of asset, a price that only goes up, friends getting rich, and easy money to join in. The South Sea Bubble is one of the oldest versions of that story, and it tends to end badly for the people who forget how the old versions ended.
